https://metro.co.uk/2023/11/13/a-naked-p.title: I did a naked photoshoot at 46 and it cured my low self-esteem
https://metro.co.uk/2023/11/13/a-naked-p.text:
Slipping off my robe, only one thought entered my mind.
‘S**t! I should have shaved.’
It was a silly thought for a number of reasons.
One – because I loved my bush. I’d never been one to care about priming myself or hair removal.
And two – I was stripping off for a naked photo shoot.
I was in a room full of people who I’d never have to see again. So what did I care if they saw my wild pubic hair?
Besides, in just a few months’ time my naked body would be on full display in my local weekly newspaper, and I couldn’t wait.
At 46 I was making a statement: I will not conform. I love my body. And yes, I am allowed to pose naked, no matter what you think.
Up until then, I had spent most of my life obsessing over my body.
In high school, having moved across the country with my dad after my parents’ divorce, I’d taken up cycling.
I became obsessed with the sport, or more accurately, loved that I could drop pant sizes effortlessly.
When I visited my mother a year later, she wrapped her arms around me and cried.
I had lost 20 pounds or more and a mother knows when something’s wrong.
If you suspect you, a family member or friend has an eating disorder, contact Beat on 0808 801 0677 or at help@beateatingdisorders.org.uk, for information and advice on the best way to get appropriate treatment
During our visit, my mom bought a video on eating disorders and made me watch it.
Out loud, I denied everything in the video – but inside my head, I checked off many of the boxes.
I wasn’t ready to give it up trying to lose weight, though.
I was still relentless and it didn’t take long for the happiness I felt at losing the weight to be replaced by an overwhelming dislike for my muscular thighs.
I hated not being able to fit into those stupid skinny jeans. I wore skirts that hid my legs and baggy clothes in general to hide myself away.
Things only got worse as I entered my twenties. I under ate; over ate; obsessed about calories.
The whole time, I cycled.
After graduating from journalism school in my early 30s, cycling became the way I saw the world.
It became my livelihood as I forged a career as a travel writer specialising in cycling – riding up mountains throughout Europe, and Peruvian peaks in incredibly thin air.
Those critical thoughts about my body disappeared on these trips.
But back home, I obsessed over gaining a few pounds – and it ruined my day; destroyed my confidence.
Gradually, I started to see my body as my instrument
By my mid 30s, the relationship with my body was still no better.
I wasn’t looking after myself.
I recall being near Paris in 2016 when my legs turned to concrete. I couldn’t move.
Realising I hadn’t eaten that day, I panicked – I was alone and my cycling trip in Europe had just begun – I couldn’t go on like this for months.
If I was going to ride, I had to eat.
Gradually, from that moment on, I started to see my body as my instrument. I had to nurture it.
And, slowly, things started to change.
When I joined a women’s only bike group in Canada in 2015 and started seeing how other women trained, joking about wobbly bits they didn’t like, it helped.
They were strong and healthy and enjoyed life – and I wanted to see my body in the way they saw theirs. Doing so allowed me to live more fully.
I participated in my first mountain bike race in 2015 and hearing the screams of friends as I pushed myself, exhausted and sweating across the finish line, was amazing.
But more incredible than that was the fact that I came in second.
‘You’re stronger than you think,’ my future husband told me. And he was right.
So in 2018, not long after the race and  just after turning  46, when I saw a call out from a local magazine asking people for their body stories, complete with a naked photoshoot, I knew I had to get involved.
I was finally ready to celebrate my body. No more slagging it off or comparing it to others’.
This would be a great way to share what I’d come through, and that now, I saw my body for what it was. Mine.
I had never felt stronger or more emotionally secure in how I looked and what I had become.
Those legs had pedalled thousands of miles, taking me through dozens of countries
Of course, that didn’t stop me from being nervous when I walked in the room.
Because it wasn’t only the shape and size of my body that had become an obsession.
Around the time my mother died in 2017, I began suffering from psoriasis.
A giant red rash developed over both my legs and it made me horribly self conscious, especially in the summer months.
If I wore a skirt or shorts, I was convinced that people would be staring at the red splotches as I walked down the street.
At first I was angry.
But after a while, I became immune to their stares and trained myself to ignore them.

I was nervous going into the photoshoot – my mouth was dry as the make-up artist gently brushed my eyelids with pink eyeshadow, and intrusive thoughts did get the best of me at first, worrying about what people would think.
But once I remembered that I had chosen to do this, I felt liberated.

Turning to the clerk, I held the picture up to her with glee.
‘This is me!’ I exclaimed. ‘Ohhh nice,’ was her polite reply.  I was ecstatic and I couldn’t wait to show everyone.
Now, I’m 51, and whenever I look at those photos, I still feel gloriously happy. That naked photo shoot was a new beginning for me.
Since then I’ve been to a nude beach for the first time with my partner, and I loved seeing so many other women of all different shapes and sizes all proud in their own skin. I’ve gone to sex clubs and felt completely natural showing off my body, all of it.

https://metro.co.uk/2023/11/11/a-friends.title: A friend’s clumsy question about my mental health taught me an important lesson
https://metro.co.uk/2023/11/11/a-friends.text:
‘I can’t live like this.’
Those were the words I said to my mum a few months ago during a severe panic attack.
She sat with me as I rode it out but afterwards, when it was over, she made me a cup of tea and asked: ‘What did you mean by that, Molly? Are you thinking about hurting yourself?’
I wasn’t, but I am glad she asked the question, even if it was hard to do.
And I want everyone to be able to have those difficult conversations, even if we don’t want to.
We are arguably more knowledgeable about mental illness than ever before.
Most of us, at the very least, know someone who is affected and want to help.
But often, the thing that holds us back is a fear of making things worse. Of saying the wrong thing.
We don’t know what to say. Specifically, we don’t know what to ask.
I’ve always noticed how people have a tendency to tiptoe around the use of certain language.
They act as if words like depression and suicide are magical incantations that will cause the person they’re talking with to develop feelings they didn’t already have – like when you tell someone not to think about a green polar bear and then that’s all they can picture.
But as someone who has struggled with mental health, I want to say: please don’t ask me if I’m feeling blue. Ask me if I’m depressed.
There’s nothing wrong with using direct language. In fact, it can be enormously helpful.
Just like the conversation I had with my mum.
At the time, I was thinking that the panic attack was never going to end.
That I would spend the rest of my life gasping for air, unable to feel anything but the terror that was gripping me.
Clarifying what I was feeling, for both mine and my mum’s sake, enabled us to decide what our next steps needed to be.
It’s OK to ask someone if they’re suffering from depression if you know the signs, or to check whether they need you to take them to their GP or the nearest hospital. Sometimes, it’s OK to just ask if they need help.
Acting like this isn’t a normal thing to do contributes to the deep stigma that exists around mental health.
As someone who has struggled for most of their life, I am of the belief that saying nothing is generally worse than saying something and getting it a little bit wrong.
Though please note, I’m not talking about saying something absolutely abhorrent like ‘just get over it’, in which case, yes, please do shut up.
Since I started opening up about my mental health journey, I’ve had numerous friends say the same thing: ‘I knew something was wrong, I just didn’t know how to approach it with you.’
To be clear, I don’t blame them at all, but I do often wonder: would I have sought help sooner if they had spoken to me about what they were seeing? If they had told me they’d noticed changes in my behaviour that they were concerned about? At the time, I didn’t know I was unwell. I had convinced myself I was fine.
When it comes to suicide in particular, asking someone if they are thinking of taking their own life might be hard, and you might struggle with how to phrase it, but you might just make all the difference. (If you think somebody is in immediate danger, you should always call 999.)
For emotional support, you can call the Samaritans 24-hour helpline on 116 123, email jo@samaritans.org, visit a Samaritans branch in person or go to the Samaritans website.
If you're a young person, or concerned about a young person, you can also contact PAPYRUS, the Prevention of Young Suicide UK.
Their HOPELINE247 is open every day of the year, 24 hours a day. You can call 0800 068 4141, text 88247 or email: pat@papyrus-uk.org.
These questions are important because they can spark honest dialogue.
That said, mental illnesses are nuanced and complicated and asking reductive questions like, ‘What caused your mental illness?’ contributes to the idea that there is a singular cause, and by extension, solution.
This is also why asking questions centred around some form of unsolicited advice is unhelpful.
This is often well-meaning; it’s natural to want to ‘fix’ someone’s pain. But offering so-called ‘solutions’ is rarely beneficial for anyone.
I once had someone very close to me ask: ‘Have you tried just thinking more positively?’
The word ‘just’ in particular felt like a stab to the heart. It minimised what I was going through. It made me feel like I was overreacting, being dramatic for struggling so deeply. It made me feel like I couldn’t talk to them about it again because it was so clear they didn’t understand mental illness at all.
For one thing, I have. Whatever you’re thinking of suggesting, I’ve tried. For another, it assumes there is a silver bullet for anxiety that I just haven’t found yet.
The day I told my mum I couldn’t live like this wasn’t my last panic attack. But thankfully, because of the journey I was already far into, they’re now fewer and further between, though no less scary.
I still have days where it’s hard to get out of bed. But now I have tools that help. I take my medication. I journal. I take cold showers and I meditate. I go to therapy.
No one is as committed to my mental health as I am.
Before you ask someone else a question, ask yourself one: am I doing this for them or for me?

Am I asking this question because I need to know if they are safe and if they aren’t I need to know how to get them to safety?
Or am I doing it because I want to make myself feel better by being ‘helpful’ and offering them a ‘quick fix’?

https://metro.co.uk/2023/11/05/i-was-in-.title: I was in a Channel 4 documentary – what happened next broke my heart
https://metro.co.uk/2023/11/05/i-was-in-.text:
‘I don’t feel proud. Sorry, I just don’t.’
These words, uttered by Nemo – my older (then 65, now 75 years old) trans friend – in 2013 broke my heart. He’s softly spoken and we were sitting in a noisy Wetherspoons having a curry.
Nemo was born in the 1940s and came out as ‘not a girl’ to his grandad when he was 14 years old after the death of his mother. As a result, his grandfather wanted him out of the way so took him to an NHS facility in Manchester and left him there.
Under the ‘care’ of the NHS, this small and scared teenager was subjected to ridiculing practices like taking his clothes off, being drugged and electro shock ‘treatment’ in the hope it would lead to hormones and surgery.
He endured this terrible treatment for two years before turning 16 years old and electing to leave the facility as soon as he realised he could. He got up and walked out of the doors with just the clothes on his back.
Nemo’s story is heartbreaking, but I am so thankful that we’ve been friends since he reached out to me after I took part in a documentary series called My Transexual Summer on C4 in 2011.
Listening to the stories of trans elders like Nemo reminds me that trans people have always existed. This is both comforting and shocking due to what they risked and endured to be themselves.
In contrast to Nemo, I was a late bloomer. I came out as trans in the dregs of my 20s, lacking the knowledge and courage to do it earlier.
The day I told my parents, I had a phone call with my mum and she told me what time they were coming over later. Suddenly, she asked if I had a cold after registering that my voice was an octave lower. At that point, I had been taking testosterone for two months – long enough to know it was the right decision for me, which was a massive relief.
I vaguely agreed that I had a sore throat (an effect of my larynx thickening) so it wasn’t technically a lie. I hung up the phone and then paced around my home for the next few hours – cleaning to distract my mind while preparing for their arrival.
When they came over, I sat them down and said ‘you know how I’ve always struggled, walked the line of gender and been very androgynous?’ My dad, not known for being overly zealous, stopped me in my tracks.
Putting his coffee down, he reassured me: ‘I think I know where you’re going with this, and I support you 100%.’ I turned to my mum and explained a bit more about my journey to be ‘me’.
With tears streaming down her cheeks (one of the only times I’d ever seen her cry) my mother initially had some concerns, but now I’m the dapper son they never knew they wanted. In fact, we attended a beach picnic this year at the first ever Trans Pride Hastings and it felt like we’d gone full circle.
Once my parents realised they weren’t losing anyone and were gaining a happy child, they started to show their support by saving articles on trans issues, attending Trans Pride events and welcoming my partner into the family.
I am one of the lucky ones.
I know that many other trans people – especially elders in our community – aren’t so fortunate. Some of them went through harrowing ordeals, such as family rejection, job loss, and electro-shock therapy just to be themselves. That’s why it’s so important to me to connect with them.
Like retired nurse Alice, who – just like myself – is keen to catch-up for lost years. Being trans often means a very non-linear life path.
After noticing Alice at various poetry and music events around Brighton and Hastings (where I spent my angsty teenage years) – often alone – I wanted to get to know her.
So I cornered her at a round table as she sat rehearsing lines to herself, waiting to go on stage to recite some new poetry. Alice was rocking her white hair (which was soon-after dyed a trademark green). Since she’d seen the reality TV series I’d been on, it felt easier for me to cut to the chase.
I bought her a whiskey and told her about co-founding an ongoing film project called My Genderation. We’d been commissioned to make 25 short films on trans lives in the UK, so Alice invited me to her one-bedroom flat and I brought my camera kit.
In the short documentary film released in 2014, she was so open and honest about her journey. In turn, the project had a transformative effect on her wellbeing by representing herself back to her.
It showed her the way I see her – as a caring, creative being. It also allowed people to get to know an otherwise shy and sensitive poet, which helped to break the ice when she’d turn up at events.
Ever since, I’ve been able to connect with more older trans people, and in 2019 I was commissioned to do a series of films about older trans people in Wales for the Trans Ageing Project called Growing Older as Me.
It’s through this series that I connected deeply with so many people, including 56-year-old trans man Dave, who found love and transitioned later in life. His story touched me because he’s from a small village in the valleys in Wales, and he’s just so matter-of-fact about who he is.
Then there’s Cat Burton, a 69-year-old retired British Airways pilot, who came out as a trans woman at the age of 58. She reminds us that, despite a fantastic career and a family, the need to be seen as ourselves is something that will always crop up and never truly goes away.
I feel blessed to have encountered some incredible gender diverse people who, despite all odds, have lived to an older age – some who are close friends.
I can’t help but wonder how many stories of trans lives have been buried though.
This feels like the first time in British history that we have trans elders that have been allowed to grow old as themselves, but society is not fully equipped to meet their needs or help them as they should.
Sadly, LGBTQ+ people at large are facing challenges in places such as nursing homes or later life care, and have even been separated from their partners or forced to go back into the closet.
Transgender people have very specific needs that need to be addressed so that they can live the last part of their life with dignity. This includes trans women who have to wear wigs, or who need to take care of their facial hair.

Trans people also often have different bodies to what’s expected and might have specific care needs as a result of various surgeries. Sadly, this isn’t necessarily knowledge that care homes have, or are equipped or trained to deal with.
As for Nemo, I know that he is haunted by memories of the clanging of the pipes and doors slamming in the communal bathroom next to his room for those two long years in the hospital. The rest of his life hasn’t been great for him either – that’s why he told me he doesn’t feel proud to be himself.

So while it’s vital to look towards the future and continue fighting for a better world for all of us, we cannot forget our trans elders and the stories of their struggles. So that, one day, they can hopefully say they finally feel proud to be themselves.

https://metro.co.uk/2023/11/27/thought-m.title: A question from a stranger on the street led to me earning thousands in my 70s
https://metro.co.uk/2023/11/27/thought-m.text:
Baffled, I sat with my group of friends around a ‘reserved’ table – covered in sparkly confetti, balloons and a Happy Birthday table banner down the middle – before it dawned on me that they had arranged a surprise 70th birthday dinner.
With a cake and candles in front of me, I looked at each beaming face and felt humbled. It was their way of saying thank you for treating them to this holiday in Tenerife.
I’m no flash sugar daddy but I didn’t have to scrimp and scrape for it, either.
So how could I afford – as a retired hospital chef – to be so generous? It all started in 2019 at the age of 65.
Walking down Peckham High Street one day, I heard someone call out: ‘Excuse me, sir!’ I ignored him but he ran in front of me with: ‘Have you ever thought of modelling?’
Seriously? At my age? He must be joking. I told him to p**s off! Usually it’s teenage girls, not pensioners like me, in market-bought jeans and a sensible anorak.
He gave me his card, then I gave him my email address and let him take my photo, thinking I’d be dining out on this story for years to come.
So six weeks later, when I got the message from him – I later learned he was called Quentin McQueen and he owned the model agency, Xdirectn – asking me to attend a photoshoot, I still thought it sounded dodgy.
I decided to go out of curiosity and turned up at the scruffy location in East London. I joined a winding queue of around 100 people.
They had asked males to wear slim-fitting black trousers and warned we’d be photographed bare-chested. After having the photos taken, they recorded my measurements.
It was an interesting day out when I had nothing better to do – but later, I got another email saying I’d passed the audition to join a modelling agency. I was flabbergasted. I didn’t know I’d even been at an audition.
Four months later on 26 July 2019, I landed my first modelling job – thanks to Quentin – which was amazingly the same date in 1971 that I’d started work for the NHS as a hospital chef before retiring in 2011 at the age of 55.
This first gig was for a high-end fashion magazine called Buffalo Zine. The clothes I wore were ridiculously expensive, but spectacular. They included a Louis Vuitton leather jacket and a £8,500 woven rubber coat.
I was also the oldest person there. The photographer got me to relax by asking me lots of mundane questions – such as ‘How did you travel here today?’, ‘What sort of music do you listen to’ – which he suggested I answer in the character of my favourite method actor, Rod Steiger.
This money has helped me take my 40 Godchildren on holidays and day trips, rather than just handing over Christmas and birthday presents
I think photographers choose me because I follow their directions to the tee. I do exactly what they tell me to do and I never moan. I simply have fun and do as I am told, even when it’s to stand in flip-flops, underwear and a towel, outdoors in freezing January!
Since then, I’ve done nudity just once, for a book about the pandemic. There was nothing salacious about it – it was more of an art project.
I exercise and stretch every day to keep trim, not just for modelling but for my health, too.
My best-paid job was for the designer, Vivienne Westwood. I received £1,000 each time and I’ve done two jobs for her.
The first was a showcase for her Autumn/Winter collection 2020, held at the Serpentine Gallery. We had to pose on tables and chairs while celebrity guests drank champagne and ate canapes.
There were a lot of celebs there, including Bianca Jagger and Vivienne herself. She was very pleasant and down to earth and displayed no airs and graces.
Unfortunately, by the time I did the second shoot for her sunglasses range, she had recently passed.
I used that cash to treat my friends to the Tenerife holiday where we celebrated my 70th. I also paid for a trip to Menorca in August with three of my godchildren – Karen and her 13-year-old daughter, Roushanna, plus Charles, who’s 43.
My other modelling jobs have included working with Clarks Shoes, Sicky Mag, Brixton Brewery (promotion for Generation Pale Ale, which was sold to raise funds for Lambeth Age UK), Central Saint Martins’ runway show for student designer Ross Palmer and a Baracuta Harrington Jacket promo. I have also been in videos for Little Runaway by Celeste and Deluded by Silas Armstrong.
This money has helped me take my 40 Godchildren on holidays and day trips, rather than just handing over Christmas and birthday presents.
I first became a Godfather just after my 16th birthday. A few of my Godchildren chose me because I go to church regularly and they got baptised as adults. Very often they then asked me to be the Godfather for their children, so l am the Godfather for the entire family.
I love my Godchildren, and I love being able to treat them all – but I never spoil them.
One Godson asked for a £600 laptop to help with homework, but I told him a £200-300 version would do the job. Another asked for Nike trainers. ‘As long as you can get them for under £50 from TK Maxx, it’s fine by me,’ I told him.
Despite my new income, I like to think that I’ve stayed humble. I have lived in the same one-bedroom flat in Brixton since 1976 and I’ve never been one to splash the cash on designer clothes or anything else. My favourite place to eat out is a greasy spoon in Woolwich.
I’m single and I don’t have lavish tastes. So what else am I going to do with the money but make precious memories with those closest to me?

https://metro.co.uk/2023/11/21/unable-co.text:
‘I’m about to turn 21, I have my whole life ahead of me, but the life I thought I’d have is gone.’
That was the prevailing thought I kept having right after being diagnosed with type 1 diabetes in 2007.
I just couldn’t cope that this was my new reality.
As a result, I experienced a nervous breakdown, trashed my room and then my housemates found me trying to hurt myself. They immediately rang my dad for help and he called 999.
It was the lowest point in my life.
Thankfully, I’m in a much better place now and I actually think my diagnosis is the best thing that ever happened to me.
I first began to experience the awful symptoms of undiagnosed diabetes during my time at university.
Focused on lectures and essays, I had no idea my immune system had destroyed the insulin-producing cells in my pancreas and that was what was causing my dramatic weight loss, blurred vision and unquenchable thirst.
I partied over Christmas and New Year, and by the time I went home to see my family in the early new year, I looked so thin that my family thought I was anorexic and so they rushed me to see my GP.
Stepping on the scales, that’s when we all discovered I weighed just six stone. This then led to a finger prick test, which showed that my sugar levels were way over the normal amount, and so I was sent to hospital.
A nurse in hospital did an artery blood test, which I remember her telling me would hurt, and not long after my diagnosis was confirmed, I was put on a saline drip to help bring my blood glucose down and started on insulin injections immediately.
‘You’ll need to do this every day for the rest of your life,’ she explained, though in all honesty it didn’t sink in at that point just how life altering this diagnosis would be.
Of course I had heard of diabetes, but I didn’t know anyone personally that had it.
Nor did I understand the difference between type 1 – which is when the pancreas can no longer make insulin as a result of your immune system attacking the cells – and type 2 – when the body becomes resistant to insulin. That knowledge came much later.
The only thing I do remember asking was: ‘Why me?’ Doctor’s couldn’t give me an answer though.
Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition – like lupus, or psoriasis – there is no widely accepted cause and it cannot be prevented. It’s just bad luck and can happen to anyone at any time in their life.
Now, it was clearly my turn.
When I returned to university, I wanted nothing more than for things to go back to normal. But they couldn’t.
I had to cut out alcohol and partying as it caused my sugars to drop too low meaning I’d start shaking, sweating and not being able to see, which in turn meant my group of friends stopped calling.
I felt isolated. Alone. And with seemingly no way out, that’s when I decided to attempt suicide.
Back in hospital I was kept overnight, but emergency wards are not designed for people in mental health crisis and I was discharged the next day because I wasn’t physically in need of A&E treatment.
I went back to my student house with very little support.
Luckily, my flatmates were there to try and help me, but I sensed they weren’t really sure what to do.

I graduated not long after somehow, but as my knowledge has grown over the years, I look back at the girl I was then and feel sorry for her – I really was just muddling my way through and I was scraping by.
I got a job as a PA in Manchester as that was all I could really cope with, and I did my best, but for the first four years I would say I was just existing rather than living.
There were lots of other challenges other than just keeping myself alive.
I had lost so much weight when I was unwell that I had lost muscle mass as well as fat. It took years of work to get this back but in the meantime my confidence was destroyed.
It’s very easy to develop disordered eating when you have to focus so much on your food and insulin intake anyway.
I struggled with diabulimia for a while – a now recognised eating disorder where people with type 1 diabetes stop taking their insulin even though doing so might kill them, because stopping means you will lose weight.
At that time though it wasn’t really widely known, and I had to deal with that myself over the course of the next few years.
A lifeline came in 2011 when I saw a diabetes specialist nurse for an appointment and just broke down at how much I was struggling.
She recognised my complete lack of knowledge of my own condition and put me on a carb counting course – where you spend five days in hospital learning about your own dosing needs and how to calculate your doses based on the amount of carbohydrates you consume.
It was a big step in the right direction, and definitely changed the course of my life with diabetes and started me off on my education journey.
The first thing it taught me was how to properly look after myself and how to accurately measure my insulin dose. But it also introduced me to other type 1s for the first time.
Sitting in a room full of other people like me was life-changing. Just being able to talk to someone else who is going through the same things you are made me feel less alone and less panicked about all the little challenges.
Relishing in that peer support that I’d been missing for so long, I then connected with the type 1 community online, and it was the amazing friends I made there that inspired me to want to give something back.
Ten years on from my diagnosis I created Type 1 Clothing – a fashion line which includes everything from dresses and jumpsuits to partywear, all designed with zips and splits to make it easier to inject insulin while in public.
Then, last year, I took part in the Channel 4 competition style reality show, Make Me Prime Minister (think, The Apprentice, but for politics) where I competed against 11 other candidates under the watch of Alastair Campbell and Baroness Sayeeda Warsi.
And I won!
I couldn’t believe it, but it meant the world to be able to show others (and prove to myself) that you don’t have to let diabetes stop you from going after your dreams.
Since then I’ve also been asked to appear alongside celebrities like global star Nick Jonas and actor Jeremy Irvine in a first-of-its-kind digital portrait exhibit on SeeDiabetes.com in celebration of World Diabetes Day.
The images capture some of the raw emotions I have experienced living with diabetes that often go unseen. And they’ll also show the world the amazing diabetes management technology I wear that supports me, day and night.
I am fortunate to be able to use a hybrid closed loop (HCL) system, which is made up of two separate devices that both monitor my glucose levels and deliver my insulin. There’s even a special AI algorithm that learns my personal patterns and adjusts my dosage accordingly.
It really has been a life changing piece of kit for me. Instead of pricking my finger multiple times a day, I can, more or less, leave it to do its thing – though I do still need to enter the carbs I eat and let it know if I’m going to exercise (yes that includes hoovering!).
While type 1 diabetes is incurable, it can be so much easier to manage now and I truly hope more people with diabetes have the opportunity to use this technology to manage their diabetes soon.
When I was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes I thought my life was over. But now, I’m part of a worldwide community and have had opportunities far greater than I ever could have imagined.
And to anyone diagnosed with diabetes now or in the future just remember, you are not alone because we have each other.

Up Next
Kim Kardashian has never been afraid of a little backlash but her nipple bra has attracted some unexpected attention from Greenpeace.
She raised eyebrows with her newest launch which is a bra with built in nipples but was quickly hit with accusations of ‘greenwashing’ in the Skims campaign video.
It’s been a rocky time for launches in the Kardashian world as Kylie Jenner’s new clothing line Khy was called out by fans for seeming to copy other designers, including ex-brother-in-law Kanye, but Kylie has not commented on the claims.
Kim has already been called out for setting a new unattainable beauty standard for women but Greenpeace took issue with her ‘mockery’ of the climate crisis.
In her launch of the product the 42-year-old cited ‘the sea levels rising’ and ‘ice sheets melting’ but promised buyers could always look cold no matter the temperature.
‘The hard truth about Kim’s new “nipple bra” 😞,’ the climate charity wrote on Instagram.
It continued: ‘Using melting glaciers and rising sea levels as a punchline to improve your profit margins makes a mockery of an issue that is devastating millions of people’s lives.
‘We desperately need global icons like Kim to champion the fight against climate change. Sadly, this isn’t what’s happening here 😢.
‘Kim’s new advert perpetuates the harmful profit-driven system accelerating the climate crisis, and diverts attention away from more impactful actions, like the UN Global Plastics Treaty, which offer a real chance for systemic change.’
Greenpeace accuses the business mogul of ‘co-opting’ the language of climate activists to promote a plastic product.
The bra is made from nylon, a thermoplastic, and spandex uses a plastic base, which means the bra will not be able to biodegrade should it be thrown away.
Skims did promise to donate 10% of sales in a one-time donation, to 1 Percent For The Planet, a global network that helps business connect with environmental organisations.
Greenpeace slammed the promise as ‘alarmingly vague’ saying it was ‘difficult to understand the impact’ the donation would make.

https://metro.co.uk/2023/11/05/look-at-o.text:
It seems we are living in a world where children submit homework generated by ChatGPT, and the specter of AI-driven unemployment looms large.
A reader has written in to cite her worry that we’ll soon become worshippers of artificial intelligence. Are we preparing to entrust everything to automation, or is there some things a machine will never be able to replicate?
Meanwhile, readers are discussing the difference between environmental protesters and footie fans, the ‘privilege’ of the OAP bus pass, Marks and Sparks paper hat burning, growing anti-Semitism and the covid inquiry.
What do you think about our readers’ letters today?
Share your thoughts in the comments.
Further to the government’s Bletchley Park summit on the issue of artificial intelligence attended by Elon Musk(Metro, Fri), it is, without doubt, startingto replace human intelligence.
In the next few years, if care is not taken, the younger generation will be unable to make crucial decisions on their own but rely absolutely on AI to do anything and everything.
As King Charles said, ‘If we are to realise the untold benefits of AI, then we must work together on combating its risks too.’
AI models have been designed to help us but we must be vigilant so that it won’t replace us and even become the gods we worship. Victoria, London

But extinction is not likely to happen, judging by my recent use of a ‘chatbot’  (to inform my energy supplier of a change of address).
It took ages to use, I had to repeat the same information to various robot ‘operators’ and, in the end, was informed that the information had been noted, which I then found was not the case.(I called my supplier and spoke to a human.) If this is AI, we aren’t in any danger. Beverley, London.
Comedy writer Andy Hamilton commented recently that the way to control AI is not to tell it where the plug is. Len, Barking
What has the world come to? Marks & Spencer has to apologise for an advert showing a burning Christmas paper hat that has colours similar to the flag of Palestine. Sudan and Kuwait have exactly the same colours.
Does M&S now have to apologise to the people of these countries as well? Gary, Essex
Sorry, this video isn't available any more.
Joyce (MetroTalk, Fri) makes a good point about how we wouldn’t tell Jews to ‘stop wallowing’ about the Holocaust like we tell black people to stop wallowing about colonial atrocities.
But I worry that this attitude is changing. On social media, the rise in anti-Semitic incidents is accompanied with phrases such as Jews ‘having it coming’ and ‘getting what they deserve’. James, London
Ryan and Beverley (MetroTalk, Tue and Thu) take issue with my complaint that Just Stop Oil protesters are treated more leniently than football fans who also stage pitch invasions. I find both of their responses full of ill-informed prejudice.
Most pitch invasions are a joyful celebration. For them to say football fans are violent is like me saying all protesters are smelly hippies who need a wash.
Ryan says Just Stop Oil are ‘always peaceful’. Try telling that to the owners of the M25 service stations that was vandalised by violent protesters causing £100,000 of damage, or the museum that had to repair the damaged Van Gogh. Maurice Fitzgerald, Worcester Park
Ted (MetroTalk, Thu) describes free travel for OAPs and the disabled as ‘privileges’.
They are not. They are tools to help people from both of those groups get through an uneven world.
If you want to treat everyone equally with transport then maybe it would be time to take a leaf out of Luxembourg’s book and provide it for free.  Capella, London
Between Boris Johnson’s reported question of whether a hair dryer up the nose would sort Covid and Donald Trump’s comment that drinking bleach would sort it, should we be more afraid that these buffoons were in charge than of the virus Amanda H, Leeds
Wouldn’t it be refreshing to hear just one witness in the Covid Inquiry own up to their part of the debacle rather than being so keen to heap blame upon others? Robert, Kent
Am I misremembering that the government was presented in 2016 with a pandemic preparation plan, which they totally ignored? Stop offering excuses for their uncaring incompetence. Valerie, London
The Covid Inquiry has heard that Mr Johnson described the virus as ‘nature’s way’ of dealing with old people. By that logic, should nature have been allowed to take its course when he had Covid? He’s no spring chicken, after all. Lizzie, Liverpool
As he is so interested in facts, could anti-Brexit Martin (MetroTalk, Fri) say which facts about the cost of joining the EU were given to the 18 to 24-year-olds polled that led to 70 per cent of them saying they wanted to do so?
Because that’s what Article 49 of the European Treaty requires – that we join, not rejoin. I would venture that they were not given any such facts and if they had been, the result could well be different. HG, Maidstone
